title: Hard-coded OLD_NFT_ID=4 and NEW_NFT_INDEX=6 give migrateMint no on-chain assurance that index 4 is decommissioned or that this contract is the canonical id-6 dispatcher — supports cross-pooler authorization hazards if multiple BalancerPoolerV2 instances are ever authorised together
description:
OLD_NFT_ID and NEW_NFT_INDEX are compile-time constants. migrateMint does NOT verify:
  (a) That `INFTMinterV2(minter).tokenIdToDispatcher(OLD_NFT_ID)` is the old (decommissioned) pooler — the index-4 dispatcher could be ANYTHING per the NFTMinterV2 admin state, including this same contract if replaceDispatcher(4, thisPooler) was ever called.
  (b) That `INFTMinterV2(minter).tokenIdToDispatcher(NEW_NFT_INDEX)` is this contract — replaceDispatcher(6, somethingElse) could leave migrateMint mintingfor an index whose 'official' dispatcher is now a different contract.
  (c) That `configs[OLD_NFT_ID].disabled == true` (i.e., that the old dispatcher has been officially decommissioned).
  (d) That `configs[NEW_NFT_INDEX].disabled == false` (the new dispatcher is the active one).

Concretely: if the protocol ever has more than one BalancerPoolerV2 contract authorised as a minter / burner on NFTMinterV2 simultaneously (e.g., during a phased rollout, or due to misconfiguration), each one with its hard-coded `OLD_NFT_ID = 4` and `NEW_NFT_INDEX = 6`, all of them will burn id-4 holdings and mint id-6 NFTs. This creates a cross-pooler 'shared minter' surface where any one of them can mutate the migration state.

The migration plan explicitly mentions deploying a *second* BalancerPoolerV2 ('BalancerPoolerV3' in plan terminology, but using the same yield-claim-nft codebase) and authorising it. Until the old pooler at index 4 has its `authorizedMinters` / `authorizedBurners` revoked, BOTH the old and new contracts could in principle execute migrateMint logic — though only the new contract has the migrateMint function (the old code did not). However, future redeploys of this codebase will all carry migrateMint with the same hard-coded constants. If a third BalancerPoolerV2 is deployed in the future (say, to fix another bug), it too will have migrateMint burning id-4 → id-6. By that time, id-4 holdings may have a different intended migration target (id-8, id-10, ...).

Additionally, this gives the protocol owner one fewer governance lever: they cannot, via NFTMinterV2 admin functions, redirect or pause migration on a per-id basis. To stop migration they must revoke the pooler's authorization. To redirect migration target they must redeploy.
exploit_path:
Scenario A — phased rollout with two new poolers authorised simultaneously:
1. Protocol decides to ship migrateMint behind a 'shadow deployment' for testing: a second BalancerPoolerV2 instance is deployed and authorised on NFTMinterV2 (e.g., to test against a forked mainnet of NFTMinterV2 state).
2. Both authorised poolers can independently call burn(holder, 4, amount). A user with id-4 holdings can call migrateMint on EITHER pooler — but only one will mint id-6 NFTs into the intended new dispatcher.
3. If the 'shadow' pooler was misconfigured (e.g., wrong setMinter target) but accidentally still authorised, user calls land on the shadow pooler and produce no usable id-6 NFTs — burn succeeds, mint succeeds, but the id-6 NFTs don't entitle the holder to anything from the canonical new dispatcher.

Scenario B — future migration to id-8:
1. Three years later, the protocol ships a new dispatcher at index 8 to retire the current id-6.
2. The hypothetical migrateMint on the new index-8 pooler would burn id-6 → id-8. But the OLD index-6 pooler (this contract) still has its migrateMint function burning id-4 → id-6.
3. A user who somehow inherited id-4 NFTs (e.g., from a long-tail wallet) calls the old pooler's migrateMint and produces id-6 NFTs at a time when id-6 has been decommissioned — those NFTs are now orphaned because configs[6].dispatcher is no longer this contract.

Neither scenario is high-likelihood; both are operational mistakes the team can avoid via revocation discipline. The finding is about the absence of a defence-in-depth check that would catch these mistakes on-chain.
mainnet_realism: Mid-life-cycle migrations are routine in long-lived protocols. The plan explicitly anticipates that the SAME codebase will be redeployed for future incidents (the 'V3' is just yield-claim-nft at HEAD; the existing codebase carries the migrateMint function for any future index swap). The OLD_NFT_ID/NEW_NFT_INDEX coupling will become a coordination tax on every future migration unless the constants are parameterised or the function is gated by tokenIdToDispatcher consistency checks.
severity_rationale: Low. The finding is defence-in-depth against an operational mistake (revocation discipline lapses, phased rollouts, future redeployments). No direct attacker exploit; all scenarios require pre-existing owner misconfiguration. Per C4: 'state handling, function incorrect as to spec' is QA / Low. The recommendation is cheap and substantially future-proofs the migration semantics; worth surfacing even at Low severity.
poc_notes: PoC outline: (1) Deploy NFTMinterV2 + two BalancerPoolerV2 instances P1 (canonical) and P2 (shadow). (2) Authorise both as burner+minter. Register P1 at index 6. (3) User holds id-4 NFTs. (4) User accidentally calls P2.migrateMint(N, recipient). Assert burn+mint succeed even though P2 is not the canonical dispatcher for id-6 — demonstrates the lack of consistency check. (5) Add the recommended `tokenIdToDispatcher(NEW_NFT_INDEX) == address(this)` check and re-run; P2.migrateMint reverts.
